section_summary: This section moves from Japanese support for Peru’s Olympic athletes to U.S. diplomatic reporting on Japanese immigration, commerce, landholding and alleged strategic activity in Peru. Its central sequence documents a major 1937 Lima press campaign portraying Japanese agricultural and commercial expansion as a threat, followed by detailed defenses of the Japanese community from T. Kurotobi and Rinuemon Takahashi. The section also includes an Associated Press report, State Department analysis, and La Prensa articles advocating immigration restrictions and protection of Peruvian agricultural land.

subfiles.title: Love for Sports; The Japanese Colony; The Next Olympic Games
subfiles.from: R. Takahashi, President of the Central Japanese Society
subfiles.about: The concluding portion of an address associates Japanese residents with Peruvian patriotic enthusiasm for the national football team and the future Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.summary: Takahashi argues sport develops a nation's physical and moral qualities, says the Japanese colony shared pride in Peru's football team and thought the Berlin decision unjust, and predicts success in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: La colonia japonesa contribuirá al envío del equipo olímpico peruano a la Olimpiada que se celebrará en Tokio
subfiles.about: The clipping reports a Central Japanese Society campaign to finance Peru’s participation in the Tokyo Olympics.
subfiles.summary: Central Japanese Society orders Japanese residents to give one sol monthly to an Olympic fund, estimated at 60,000 soles a year, to send Peru's team to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4978: Map of Peru Printed in Lima by Japanese for Use of Their Nationals
subfiles.from: Fred Morris Dearing, American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: The embassy transmits a Japanese-language map of Peru printed in Lima in 1924.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 4978: Dearing forwards a map of Peru printed in Lima by Japanese for their nationals; maps showing boundaries need government approval, which is unknown.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4983: Japanese Penetration in Peru
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus, Jr., for the Ambassador, American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: The embassy forwards an Associated Press report on Japanese immigration and colonization that the Peruvian censor had suppressed.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains that most of the report’s information had already appeared in earlier embassy reporting. It was nevertheless transmitted because Luis León stated that Peruvian censors had blocked foreign publication on the ground that the article was not in Peru’s interest.

subfiles.title: Japanese Colonization / Peruvian-Japanese Commercial Relations
subfiles.from: Luis León, Associated Press representative in Lima
subfiles.to: Associated Press and intended news readership
subfiles.about: A proposed news report portrays Japanese immigration, non-assimilation and trade as harmful to Peru and explains the government’s quota measures.
subfiles.summary: AP report alleging Japanese residents stay separate, educate children as Japanese subjects and remit capital, with the 1936 quota aimed at them; also links the abrogated 1929 treaty to textile competition.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Penetration in Peru
subfiles.from: R. A. Chapin, Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Ambassador Steinhardt’s report on the Lima campaign against Japanese immigration and economic expansion.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on aroused Peruvian opinion and the alleged progression of Japanese immigrants from laborers to merchants and manufacturers, with statistics on small businesses and possible new restrictions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 245: Newspaper Campaign against Japanese Infiltration in Peru
subfiles.from: Laurence A. Steinhardt, American Ambassador to Peru
subfiles.about: Steinhardt reviews the 1937 Lima press campaign against Japanese immigration, landholding and commercial expansion and the Japanese community’s replies.
subfiles.summary: The despatch identifies Guillermo Salinas Cossío as a principal author in a campaign that depicted Japanese economic expansion as a path toward political domination. It summarizes letters and articles alleging Japanese advantages in finance, mutual aid, land acquisition, retailing, cotton production and community organization, while also noting rebuttals from Japanese spokesmen H. Ikeyama and Aki Banno. Steinhardt reports that the government was considering stronger restrictions and connects its policy to Peru’s Buenos Aires conference proposal and the closure of the Peruvian consulate in Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Political Report: Anti-Japanese Feeling in Peru
subfiles.from: Homer Brett, American Consul General, Callao-Lima
subfiles.about: Brett analyzes rising anti-Japanese feeling and introduces two Japanese New Year statements intended to answer criticism of the colony.
subfiles.summary: Brett reports popular accusations of non-assimilation, commercial displacement and remittances, discounts a military settlement plan, and links anxiety to the China war and failed cultural diplomacy.

subfiles.title: Peruvian Prosperity and the Conflict in the Far East
subfiles.from: T. Kurotobi, President of the Central Japanese Society of Peru
subfiles.to: Peruvian people and readers of El Comercio
subfiles.about: Kurotobi offers New Year greetings and defends Japanese immigrants’ contribution to Peruvian agriculture, commerce and employment.
subfiles.summary: Kurotobi praises President Benavides and argues that Japanese residents regard Peru as a second homeland, using his own rise from plantation laborer to merchant and landowner as evidence. He supplies population figures for Japanese communities throughout Peru and describes their work in agriculture, cafés, barbershops, bakeries, bazaars, fishing and trades. He denies that Japanese businesses displaced Peruvians and emphasizes investment, local employment, low prices, hygiene and service.

subfiles.title: Our Mission in the Promotion of Peruvian-Japanese Economic Relations
subfiles.from: Rinuemon Takahashi, President of the Japanese Association of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.to: Peruvian people and readers of La Prensa
subfiles.about: Takahashi argues that Peru and Japan are economically complementary and proposes closer commercial cooperation and a Peruvian mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Takahashi presents Japanese merchants, manufacturers and farmers as collaborators in Peru’s economic development and denies that they receive organized or governmental financial support. He argues that Peru’s raw materials and Japan’s manufacturing economy create a mutually beneficial trade relationship, citing cotton, wool and minerals. He proposes an economic mission to Japan and offers association assistance with closer commercial and industrial ties; the article was datelined January 3 and published January 4.
keywords: Japanese Association of Commerce and Industry

subfiles.title: La infiltración japonesa I: La colonia japonesa y la producción agrícola
subfiles.about: Salinas Cossío warns that Japanese acquisition of cotton land threatens Peru’s economic independence and urges enforcement of restrictions on foreign tenancy.
subfiles.summary: La Prensa article: Salinas Cossio says Japanese land acquisition is the most consequential infiltration, with a substantial share of Peruvian cotton, and urges enforcing the 80-percent limit on foreign yanaconazgo.

subfiles.title: La colonia japonesa y la producción agrícola
subfiles.about: The editorial endorses Salinas Cossío’s warning about Japanese acquisition of the coastal cotton lands and describes the colony as a separate nationality within Peru.
subfiles.summary: La Prensa editorial: public approval of Salinas Cossio's article shows alarm over Japanese agriculture, a nationality within another nation; frank recognition is needed for friendship.
